connector: Most children long ago did not go to school. So how did they learn? Today’s article has two paragraphs. Look for what each paragraph is about, and the one big idea that fits both.

a.raw: in the town of york a baker hired an apprentice
a.fixed: In the town of York, a baker hired an apprentice.
a.why: In starts the sentence, so it gets a capital I. York is the name of a place. A comma comes after the opening part, In the town of York. A period ends the sentence.

b.raw: in old london master hugh taught his apprentice
b.why: In starts the sentence. London is a place. A comma comes after the opening part. Master is a title right before his name, Hugh. A period ends the sentence.

vcloze1.h1: This young person is learning a trade from a master.
vcloze1.why: An apprentice learns a trade by working for an expert.

vcloze2.h1: This person already knows the trade and makes things by hand.
vcloze2.why: A craftsman is a skilled worker.

vcloze3.h1: This is a food: a thick soup.
vcloze3.why: Pottage is a thick soup of vegetables and grains.

vcloze4.h1: This one is something you do with a needle and thread.
vcloze4.why: To embroider is to sew pictures onto cloth.

cards.title: Job Spotlight: The Apprentice
cards.sub: A real job in the Middle Ages
cards.todo: Read about this real job. Then read the two questions and the article.
text: An apprentice lived with a master and learned a trade, like baking or blacksmithing.
Many started at about twelve to fourteen years old and stayed about seven years.
To finish, some made a special piece of work to show the guild. That is where the word masterpiece comes from.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back, it’s Opti. Long ago, most children did not go to school. So how did they learn a job? Today’s article tells you, in two paragraphs.
transcripts.guide1: Word study. Match trans words to their meanings, tap every word that needs a capital, and find the word that splits between two consonants.
transcripts.guide2: Read about servants and apprentices. Then watch my video in the Read Like a Writer box.
transcripts.guide3: Today you write a research question and take notes from two articles.

notes.wordParts: The word part trans means across. transport = to carry across. translate = to carry words across into another language. Some words only start with t r a n, like tranquil (calm).
notes.grammar: Capital letters start every sentence and every important word in a name: people (Queen Eleanor), places (Tower of London) and titles. Small words like the, of and in stay small inside a name or title, unless they come first.
notes.spelling: VCCV means vowel, consonant, consonant, vowel. Split the word between the two consonants: bas · ket, tun · nel. Letters like ph and th stay together.
notes.wgrd: When an article has two paragraphs, ask what each one is mostly about. Then find one big idea that fits both.
vocab: a person learning a trade by working under an expert
a skilled worker who makes things by hand
a thick soup of vegetables and grains
to decorate cloth with needle and thread

mods.todo: Tap the yellow parts. Then pick Sentence A or B and type it the right way.
mods.script: Let's fix a sentence. Look at the correct one first. In medieval England, an apprentice might work for Master Thomas for seven years. See the comma after England? It ends the opening part. And Master Thomas gets two capitals: one for the title, one for the name. Tap the yellow parts. Then pick Sentence A or Sentence B, and type it the right way.

mods.todo: Read the poem out loud. Then say how it is different from a lie.
mods.script: Here's a funny poem by Edward Lear, written long ago. Read it out loud. Could two owls, a hen, four larks and a wren really nest in one beard? No way! Lear stretches the truth on purpose. That's called hyperbole. Now think: how is this different from a lie? Say your answer out loud.

mods.todo: Tap a word, then tap what it means. Match all four words.
mods.script: Remember, trans means across. Here's a long one that's not on your list. Transcontinental. Find trans at the front. A continent is a giant piece of land. So a transcontinental train goes all the way across it! Read the Remember box. Then tap a word, and tap what it means. Match all four words.

mods.todo: Fill in each sentence with a word from the word bank. Tap Check My Work. Then play the matching game.
mods.script: Here's a word from the world of trades. Guild. A guild was a club for one kind of worker, like all the bakers in a town. Read each sentence with a bank word in the blank. If it makes sense, keep it. Then play the matching game.

mods.todo: Read the Remember box. Then tap every word that needs a capital.
mods.script: Spot the capitals with me. abbot peter walked to bath abbey. Abbot starts the sentence, and it's his title. Peter is his name. Bath Abbey is a place, so both words get capitals. That's four! Read the Remember box. Then tap every word that needs a capital.

mods.todo: Read the rule. In each row, tap the word with two consonants in the middle.
mods.script: Use your eyes for this one. Sofa. Pony. Doctor. Which one has two consonants between its vowels? Doctor! O, then c and t, then o. Doc. Tor. Read the rule. Then in each row, tap the one word with two consonants in the middle.

mods.label: Opti shows you how
mods.script: [warmly] Let's try all three parts with a different sentence from today's article. Poor children worked in the fields or served in the homes of nobles. Part one, read like a reader. Poor children had jobs, in the fields or in a noble's home. Part two, read like a writer. The little word or joins two choices, and both halves have the same shape: worked in, served in. Part three, mimic. Here's mine: Opti worked in the library or perched in the old oak. Now it's your turn with the apprentice sentence. Write one sentence in each box.

mods.todo: Answer each question in full sentences. Use details from the article.
mods.script: Now answer in full sentences. One, what is the central idea? Say it in one sentence. Two, name one way boys and girls were alike, and one way they were different. Three, does Jemmy's job seem real, based on the article? Use one detail.

virtue.name: diligence
virtue.title: Diligence Watch: Is someone working hard?

items.t: An apprentice worked for a master craftsman for several years, learning every part of the job.
items.why: He kept at it for years until he knew the whole job.

items.t: In the Middle Ages, most children did not go to school.
items.why: That tells what children did not do. It is not about someone working.

items.t: Girls learned to weave and sew.
items.why: Weaving and sewing take patient, careful work.
